description: Las cabras que ganaran el nasa space app challenge
summary:
MARSCEPTION finds places on Earth that look like the lunar south pole and Jezero Crater on Mars, shows how similar they really are, and turns them into a game.

We built a crater detector that reads elevation data from Earth, the Moon and Mars at the same resolution, using ESA Copernicus, NASA LRO LOLA and NASA MOLA maps. An explainable model trained on thousands of real lunar and Martian craters scores each crater-like spot on Earth, and NASA POWER climate and MODIS vegetation data complete the comparison.

In the game, you pick one of those places, build a rover on a budget, test it on the site's real terrain, fix what fails, and then deliver cargo under real lunar or Martian gravity.

Astronauts and rovers train at places like these before they fly. MARSCEPTION makes them open and playable, and it is honest about what Earth can't recreate: gravity, vacuum, radiation and air pressure.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Before a rover goes to the Moon or Mars, it is tested on Earth. But what will that test miss? MARSCEPTION answers using open NASA & ESA data in two connected parts:

1. An analog finder. It searches arid regions on Earth for hollows shaped like craters near the lunar south pole (the Artemis candidate region) and Jezero Crater on Mars. For each candidate, it compares the same variables in the same units on Earth and at the destination, listing what Earth cannot test.

2. A 2D rover game. Select the Moon or Mars as your destination, open a real Earth analog's site file, and build a robot within a 1,000-credit budget to traverse the site's actual elevation profile. If the rover becomes immobilized in challenging terrain like dunes, players receive feedback explaining the failure and are encouraged to revise the design. Through this cycle, players learn how gravity and environmental differences affect rover performance, gaining experience delivering cargo under authentic lunar or Martian gravity.

Why crater shapes: the Artemis candidate region at the lunar south pole is ringed by craters whose permanently shadowed floors may hold water ice, so a base there will need rovers that can drive down crater walls and across their floors. On Mars, Jezero itself is a crater, and Perseverance has driven its floor and climbed its rim. Earth hollows with the same shape let teams rehearse those drives; Earth cannot reproduce the polar shadow, the cold, or the ice.

HOW IT WORKS

- One detector, three worlds: the same algorithm runs on elevation data resampled to 200 m for Earth (ESA Copernicus DEM GLO-30), the Moon (NASA LRO LOLA), and Mars (ESA/NASA HRSC and MOLA). It finds 9 of 11 known Mexican craters and 40% of a wider set of 62 known Mexican volcanic craters (15 misses hold lakes, which the elevation model sees as flat water). A vegetation mask from NASA's MODIS satellites keeps only dry terrain, leaving 296 candidates across Mexico and one 600 × 600 km area each in the Atacama Desert, Arizona, and western Arabia.

- Explainable model: a logistic regression trained on 4,288 lunar and 573 Martian craters estimates whether an Earth hollow's shape is more Moon-like or Mars-like, and how far it is from both. Balanced accuracy (the average of its hit rates on Moon craters and on Mars craters) is about 78% when tested on areas left out of training, and 70–92% on an unseen Mars site. Depth-to-diameter (how deep a crater is for its width) alone gets 76%.

- Comparator: temperature range and precipitation (NASA POWER), vegetation (MODIS), and slope, compared with the destination (temperatures from Perseverance's MEDA and LRO's Diviner), with a vegetation veto. All three negative controls (places that should not match: Amazon, Congo, Mekong rice plain) score zero. Of 21 known analogs, 9 pass against Jezero and 2 against the steeper lunar south pole; the rest are analogs for reasons these variables do not measure, like polar cold or caves.

- Method check: in the regions we scanned, partly chosen because they contain known sites, the detector's candidates include El Pinacate (Mexico) and Colton Crater (Arizona), where the Apollo 14 and 15 crews trained, found without being given their locations. El Pinacate's El Elegante crater ranks 12th of 296 by raised rim (the ridge around a crater's edge), and its shape rates 97% Moon-like. Colton is weaker: our rim measure does not confirm it, and only the AI label calls it a crater. These cases support the method; they are not a discovery or a full validation.

- To clarify how analogs are selected: the 296 candidates are crater-shaped hollows, not analogs. AI-assisted labels count 27 natural craters and 53 mines; the AI was checked against sources in only 33 cases (29 correct), all mines, volcanoes, or Meteor Crater. From the natural craters, we propose two volcanic craters in Saudi Arabia for field verification, chosen by shape, not geology. For Mars, the Jabal Bayda tuff ring (a low crater built by steam-driven volcanic explosions): its shape rates 85% Mars-like, and at 1.03 km wide and 22 m deep, it matches a crater in the Gale region, where the Curiosity rover landed (1.06 km, 22 m). For the Moon, the Al Wahbah maar (a crater blasted out where rising magma met groundwater) is 65% Moon-like; at 2.19 km wide and 159 m deep, it matches a crater near the lunar south pole (2.18 km, 157 m). Neither is in the global database of Ryan et al. (2024, Geosphere), which covers basaltic fields only and is not exhaustive, and we did not find either used as a Moon or Mars analog in the literature we reviewed; Al Wahbah is published as an analog for Saturn's moon Enceladus (Dos Santos et al. 2024, Astrobiology). Open-pit mines such as Cananea are proposed as operational analogs (steep walls, excavation, shadowed floors), not geological ones.

- Real physics: each level is an unstretched window of a real elevation profile. Traction and sinkage use standard wheel–soil equations (Mohr–Coulomb, Bekker–Wong) with Apollo lunar and Viking Martian soil values, so wider wheels sink less and push harder. Gravity is 9.81, 3.71, and 1.62 m/s². Game-only values (prices, part stats, tread factor) are marked (P) for provisional.

- Seven featured tests: the five highest-similarity playable sites, one per kind of place, plus Samalayuca and Rincón de Parangueo for variety: the Samalayuca dunes (wind-built like Martian dunes, but quartz sand), the Pinacate lava fields, the Cananea copper pit, the Jabal Bayda tuff ring, the dry Rincón de Parangueo maar (a shape-only match to lunar south pole craters), and two known impact craters used as positive controls: Tenoumer in the Sahara (where the level adds dust whirlwinds like Jezero's) and Pingualuit in Arctic Canada (snow, ice, and February daily lows averaging −34 °C).

- Discover maps the catalog with "Why here?" provenance for each site. ANA, the analog tutor, answers suggested questions offline; optional live AI answers are labeled and can be wrong.

BENEFITS

- Answers "Where on Earth is most like this place, how alike is it, and where does the analogy break?"

- Teaches the test-fail-redesign loop and why gravity and soil change how a rover moves, in minutes, in English or Spanish.

- Open and reproducible: the catalog, methodology, validation, and code are public.

INTENDED IMPACT

An open catalog that can grow to more arid regions and user-proposed sites, giving analog researchers a same-method shortlist to verify in the field, starting with Jabal Bayda and Al Wahbah. In the field, a team preparing a rover test could open a site file before traveling to see what the place can train (driving in loose sand and up dune crests at Samalayuca, steep walls at Cananea, moving inside a crater at Jabal Bayda) and what it cannot (gravity, vacuum, radiation). For classrooms, a game where students test a rover against real terrain, soil, and gravity values. For example, a class can send a rover with standard wheels onto the Samalayuca dunes, watch it get stuck, switch to wide wheels, and see why spreading the weight lets it cross. In the game, ground pressure drops from about 8 to 5 kPa. A Mexican case study, our most complete validation, brings Pinacate, Samalayuca, and Rincón de Parangueo into the space exploration conversation.

TOOLS

Google Earth Engine, Python, NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, JSON Schema, FastAPI, JavaScript, React, Vite, MapLibre, Phaser 3, Matter.js, Playwright, FFmpeg, Git and GitHub. AI coding assistants: Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, declared in the AI disclosure. ANA's optional live answers use the OpenAI API. Pixel-art effects use pixelfx (MIT License, © 2026 Patch and Hugo Duprez). No special hardware: any modern browser on a computer or phone.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Analog studies usually end in a map or a table. We added a way to feel the difference: the same rover handles differently on Earth, the Moon, and Mars because the physics uses real soil and gravity values. The game is built around failing on Earth on purpose, so players learn why a design works before the real mission. Our team composed the in-game soundtrack and recorded the title voice; the trailer's edit and score were AI-assisted. Our team made the pixel art with AI assistance.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty: no invented data, missing values stay missing, game values are marked (P), and we say "candidates" not "discoveries".

- Fairness: the same code and resolution on all three worlds.

- Validation: positive controls (known craters), negative controls (rainforest, farmland), and spatially grouped validation so nearby craters do not leak between training and testing.

- Limits: gravity, vacuum, radiation, and air pressure are stated on every site file and on the mission results screen.

- Practical limits: 200 m maps miss small features and craters under 0.6 km; the search covers Mexico and 3 of 10 priority arid regions, not the whole planet; shape similarity says nothing about rock composition; the proposed sites have not yet been checked in the field; and the game's Earth sand is generic dry sand, not measured at each site, whereas Mars sinkage uses a lab soil simulant (M90), not real Martian soil.

- Accessibility: keyboard and touch, three ways to build the robot (drag, tap, or keyboard), English and Spanish, and offline play without the API.

NASA POWER – Climate data for Earth sites
NASA Mars 2020 Perseverance MEDA – Jezero weather
projectRefs: Pelletier et al. 2015 – Dune slip-face angles
